description: GeoHarmonix is building a 26-year cross-sensor (MODIS + VIIRS) harmonized active-fire archive & Burning Activity Calendar using NASA FIRMS satellite data. We combine orbital mechanics, physics-based footprint calibration, and modern interactive 3D web visualization to eliminate multi-sensor distortion and reveal true climate trends. Passionate about Earth observation, wildfire analytics, AI/ML, and geospatial tech? Join us to make satellite fire data universally accessible!
summary:
GeoHarmonix is a web workbench that makes 26 years of NASA fire detections comparable across satellites. NASA FIRMS records fires with two sensor families, MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS sees much smaller fires, so counts jump when it joins: over India, Bangladesh and Myanmar, raw detections rose 1,293% from 2005 to 2024, largely a sensor effect.

We harmonize the two records by removing South Atlantic Anomaly noise, re-classifying day and night by sun angle, and fitting a correction tested on years it never saw. The harmonized trend is about +3.0% per year, and the MODIS-VIIRS distribution gap (KS distance) falls from 0.115 to 0.035. We also report a limit: fire-power error is not reliably improved.

Users explore NASA satellite imagery with H3 hexagon bins, search any state, and open a Sensor Laboratory, burning calendar and a live NASA feed with real satellite orbits, in English and Hindi.

It matters because fire, air-quality and climate decisions need trends that reflect fire, not changing sensors.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

GeoHarmonix turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire data from two satellite families, MODIS (Terra/Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), into one consistent fire record. Raw counts jump whenever a new sensor joins (we measured a false +1,311% step in the Mekong), so naive trends are wrong.

HOW IT WORKS

Our pipeline (1) rebuilds each detection's real footprint from scan angle (a MODIS edge pixel is 74x larger than a VIIRS nadir pixel), (2) allocates energy onto the Uber H3 hexagon grid, (3) re-classifies day/night by sun angle, (4) removes South Atlantic Anomaly noise, (5) calibrates fire power in two stages, (6) merges multi-satellite overpasses into fire episodes, and (7) normalizes by observation effort. The output is a 26-year x 73-pentad Burning Activity Calendar with a standardized anomaly index.

RESULTS (3.3 million real NASA detections)

Mekong's 2024 step shrinks from 1,411 to 90.5 on a 2005=100 index; the Amazon's from 814 to 37.7. On 20,786 coincident MODIS-VIIRS pairs, the distribution gap falls 69% (KS 0.115 to 0.035) and R2 rises from 0.784 to 0.805. We also report what did not work: the fire-power holdout interval includes zero, so we claim no reliable gain there.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE AND ADVANCED

- A dual-system AI harness (LangGraph): a fast decision model plus a reasoning model, 18 deterministic tools, a numeric-grounding verifier that checks every number against data, and human sign-off.

- A live NASA panel: latest FIRMS detections over real GIBS satellite imagery, with real satellite orbits and next-pass times computed from public orbital elements.

- Interactive workbench: H3 hexagon map, state-by-state search, regional intelligence charts, a Sensor Laboratory, in English and Hindi.

TOOLS

Python 3.11, NumPy, pandas, H3, Pydantic, LangGraph, FastAPI, pytest (186 tests), ruff, pyright; TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Three.js, Tailwind, next-intl; NASA FIRMS, GIBS, CelesTrak; GitHub Actions, Vercel.

IMPACT AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Fire agencies, air-quality and climate researchers can trust that a rising trend means more fire, not a new sensor. We designed for honesty (no burned-area or calibration claims we cannot support), reproducibility (cached data, deterministic runs, tests) and access (bilingual, no login).
